subject: robotBarista
pitch:
Category: Humanoid character.
Subject: robot barista.
Style: Portal (Aperture Science).
reasoning:
I'm planning a single TypeScript module for an Aperture Science-style robot barista, thinking through the design carefully given the SDK constraints and aiming for a manageable but rich implementation—white panels, orange accents, black joints, glowing eye.

For the look I'm picturing a humanoid with a spherical camera-eye head, apron with Aperture logo, one hand holding a cup labeled "Test Subject Blend" and the other a portafilter, plus a barista cap and antenna light.

Now I'm sketching the skeleton: hips at root height, a spine chain up through chest and neck to head, legs running hip-knee-ankle, and arms branching shoulder-elbow-wrist into simplified fingers, while keeping total joint count within the 160 limit.

For the head I'll add a small jaw plate under the eye with a speaker-grille slit so it reads as a mouth, and for the rest pose I'm settling on a relaxed A-pose with arms angled outward, fingers spread, and the cup resting naturally in one open hand.

Settling on bent elbows with forearms forward and palms up—a natural pose for holding props. Right hand will cradle the cup resting on its open palm, and I'm considering what small item the left hand should hold, maybe a pastry.

Now I'm working out body proportions and joint coordinates — setting floor level, hip height, knee and ankle positions, and torso placement to build a stylized figure around 1.75 units tall.

Checking the leg lengths against the hip-to-ankle distance confirms a slight bend is needed, so I'll use two segments summing just over the straight distance and bend toward +Z. I'm naming the chain joints by side, with left mapped to positive X and parented to the hips root, then moving on to defining the spine using Catmull points.

For the spine I'm setting the root joint at the hips with no parent, then building a three-span chain up through spine1, spine2, and chest using interpolated points toward shoulder height, keeping the base spine1 joint coincident with the hips position. Now I'm sketching the neck chain as a short two-point segment rising from the chest to the head base.

I'm working out the head placement, deciding to use region-based positioning with model-space coordinates (x left, y up, z forward) rather than fiddling with bone direction vectors, since that gives a simpler way to orient the head without worrying about local axis alignment.

Now I'm thinking about how to construct the torso, considering whether to loft or sweep the shape.

I'll use a box-sectioned sweep along the spine chain for that blocky robot look, with half-extent radii. For the Portal-style paint, I'm thinking white panels with thin grey seam lines, slight AO shading, and orange scuff marks rather than rivets.

Writing panel seam shader...

For glow, I'm considering importing a glow kit but painted parts can't actually glow so I'll give them a flat color instead. Now thinking through the eye design—likely a lens built from a circle or sphere with a dark rim and glowing iris, deciding between orange/amber or blue tones based on classic robot-eye color conventions like Aperture's turret red or Atlas's blue.

I'll go with warm amber for the eye, giving it a GLaDOS-like friendly glow with ring segments. For the Aperture-style logo decal on the apron, I'm sketching an SVG approximation with a ring and rotated trapezoid blades to mimic the aperture shutter look, then planning the apron itself as a textured box part in charcoal with orange trim, pockets, stitching, and a "CAFÉ SCIENCE" label on the front face.

Since BoxGeometry repeats the texture on every face, I realize a plane decal layered on the front is cleaner for the apron graphic, positioned just in front of the torso surface at the appropriate z-depth. I'm reworking the torso into separate pelvis and chest boxes for a blockier puppet look rather than one continuous taper, deciding rigid parts are fine for rest pose while leaving room for a spine-chain sweep later if bending is needed.

Now I'm realizing the torso tapers at an angle, so a flat apron plane would intersect the body rather than sit flush — I need the apron to conform to the sweep surface instead, using a decal projection that wraps the texture onto the geometry directly with transparency outside the printed region.

Then I add a sweep loop at the waist with a thin charcoal/orange radius, applied only to the torso, and double-check whether the decal projection needs sufficiently dense surface triangles to project onto correctly.

Maybe simpler to assemble the torso from multiple box pieces instead, giving more control over the blocky Portal-style panel look — chest plate, back panel, shoulder bumps, abdomen band, and an orange stripe accent. For the head, I want that Aperture sentient-robot aesthetic.

Checking the curvature math so the eye lens plane sits flush against the visor's curved surface rather than floating above it at the edges.

I'm also reconsidering whether a single centered eye (Portal-style) or a pair of eyes reads as friendlier for a barista robot design -- two eyes with a rounded head feel more approachable.

I'll go with two round glowing amber eyes on a black visor, maybe with a segmented iris look, and add simple white lid plates above them on hinge joints so the face can tilt expressively without too much rig complexity.

For the mouth, I'm adding a small chin piece below the visor with a dark horizontal-slit grille to suggest a speaker/mouth, mounted on its own jaw joint that can rotate forward.

Now I'm working out proportions: shortening the neck, setting torso top around 1.33 with a black ring joint connecting to a head centered near 1.58 with radius ~0.18, giving a cute oversized-head look topped by the antenna reaching toward 1.9.

For accessories, I'm settling on round dark ear discs with orange rings, a small antenna with an orange bulb, and a name tag on the apron instead of a hat or headset. I'm plotting the arm joints too, tracing shoulder to elbow to wrist coordinates so the forearm angles forward and slightly upward.

I'm structuring the arm as a simple shoulder-elbow-wrist polyline chain with sharp bends at each joint, using the wrist as the tip joint aimed forward so the hand and fingers can be built off it, parented to that same chain.

Now I'm detailing the robot joints—black spheres at shoulder and elbow like a Portal-style robot—and tapering the upper arm and forearm capsules with an orange cuff band near the wrist, plus a white shoulder pad cap. For the hand, I'm positioning the palm as a box extending forward from the wrist.

Working out finger joints and positions...

I'm picking a white palm with dark grey fingers for contrast, and now placing a cup prop on the right palm—a lathe-built paper cup with lid and orange sleeve texture, rigged to the wrist bone with proportions roughly 0.12 tall, tapering from 0.032 to 0.038 radius.

Checking the geometry, I realize the fingers curling under or around the cup base would intersect it slightly given their radius and position, so I'm adjusting the finger curl upward to wrap around the cup without clipping into its bottom surface.

Now shifting to the left hand: I'm planning a plate with a cake slice resting on the palm — a lathe-generated disc for the plate, and an extruded wedge shape for the cake slice, topped with frosting, a cherry, and a small glowing candle.

Thinking through the full scene now: chocolate cake with white icing and a glowing candle, sitting on a white plate with an orange ring, resting on an open palm. I'm working out the geometry so fingers curling around the plate edge don't intersect the disc, positioning the plate as a thin lathe disc above the palm with fingers placed just beside it at staggered x-offsets.

Checking the A-pose arm placement: forearms extend forward at waist height, with shoulders at x=0.27 and elbows reaching x=0.33, keeping clear of the torso width and the cup positions. I'm working through the coordinates for elbow and wrist joints to confirm the arm path from shoulder down stays clear of the body.

Now I'm designing the legs: thin ankles, white thigh panels, black knee spheres, and chunky shoes with white uppers and orange soles, tapering thigh and shin radii and placing a knee sphere at the joint. For the feet, I'm sizing a box shape to sit flush with the floor, adjusting the vertical center so the sole touches y=0.

I'm then adding foot details—a rounded toe sphere, a thin dark sole strip, and white foot body above it—followed by shaping the pelvis with rounded box sweeps and a black waist belt loop around the hip joint.

I like the idea of giving this character a cute espresso-machine backpack for a barista vibe: a white box pack with copper pipe sweeps, a small pressure gauge, and an orange tank, keeping to the simple white/black/orange palette.

Writing glow helper function...

I'll avoid the module-import risk and reimplement glow myself using THREE directly, caching cloned materials by key instead of relying on the kit's export path. Now I'm planning the texture set needed: an eye texture with iris and highlight, an apron texture with logo and pocket details, and an aperture logo for the sleeve/chest/back, while noting the lathe-based cup geometry may only support paint rather than UV-mapped textures.

So for the cup I'll go with a flat orange lathe material plus a decal carrying the logo, since decals can conform to lathe geometry. I'm also listing remaining textures: a gauge face, a speaker grille for the mouth, and a small playful name tag reading something like "Hello, I am CAFF-1 / Please do not drink the neurotoxin," skipping any menu board idea, and considering hazard stripe paint (orange-black) for a belt or cuff band instead of a texture card.

I'm planning paint variants for the white body panels, a grain-textured orange, and black rubber, plus optional serial/backpack-label decals like "CAFFEINE ENRICHMENT CENTER" or "AS-ESPRESSO 9000," skipping a warning sticker idea. That brings the texture count to around seven (eye, apron, logo, gauge, grille, tag, backpack label), and I'm targeting roughly 150-250 parts using repeated helper geometry like fingers, keeping flat colors under twenty since paints don't count against that limit, starting the palette with a soft white base color for panels.

I'm fleshing out the rest of the palette now—charcoal, black, two oranges (a standard and an Aperture-style orange), amber for the eye glow, copper, steel, cream, chocolate brown, cup-white, coffee brown, cherry red, and a blue accent for small status lights on the backpack and antenna, mixing orange and blue Portal-style highlights for the shoulder trims and pack indicators. Writing paint helper code...

Finishing the seam shading logic, then noting that since surfaces are curved the seam pattern will naturally bend with the geometry, which is fine for this panel look.

For the head, panel paint would look odd on a plain sphere, so I'm sketching a dedicated head paint function that places seams along polar angles instead — a vertical center seam plus an equator band — reusing the same seam-detection approach but centered on the head's own coordinates.

Defining orange paint shading and hazard stripe patterns...

Now I'm sketching out the API structure, starting with the builder call and the root hip joint as the rig's base.

Then I'm defining the spine chain as a polyline path with named segments (spine1, spine2, chest), and setting up a torso sweep driven by the chain's roll.

I should use flat caps instead of round for the torso sweep, since a round cap would add an unwanted dome of extra height at the shoulders. I'm setting the radius profile along the torso path: narrower at the hip, tapering in slightly at the waist, then widening toward the chest and shoulders, ending in a flat plane at the top for the shoulders.

Now I need to connect the legs at the hip where the torso's flat bottom cap sits at y=0.88, and I'm considering adding a small pelvis block or joint piece there so the leg sockets don't look like they're floating inside the torso.

For the legs themselves I'm sweeping each as a single tapered tube running from hip down to ankle, with radii keyed at a few points along the chain so the knee bulges slightly before narrowing toward the foot.

I'm checking that chain accepts names, role, and bends arrays for inner joints, confirming the returned joint points can be indexed directly for placement, like using leg.joints[1].at to position a sphere at the knee.

Now I'm figuring out the foot placement: using the last joint in the chain as the ankle/tip, then sketching the foot geometry as a combination of box shapes for the shoe upper plus a sphere for the toe.

Still defining geometry...

Now I'm setting up the arm chains with shoulder-elbow-wrist joints parented to the chest, tapering radii along each segment and smoothing the elbow corner so the limb reads as a continuous rounded form.

For coloring, I'm thinking through whether to apply a split-band scheme along the arm—white panel on the upper arm transitioning to a darker charcoal cuff near the wrist—using banded color keys along the sweep parameter instead of a single flat tone.

I'm also planning joint details: dark spheres at shoulders and elbows for articulation points, a white pauldron-style cap at the shoulder, and a thin orange ring accent around the upper arm for visual contrast.
